title: Digital Design Lab
text:
Preface
Every processor, controller, and screen you have ever used began as a handful of logic gates someone arranged on purpose. This book is about learning to do that arranging yourself — not by reading about it, but by designing, simulating, and running your own digital circuits on real hardware.
Over nine labs, you will go from your first combinational circuit to a complete FPGA-based System on Chip: a HIPV, a Risc-V based processor, talking to peripherals you wrote, over a bus you configured, validated with a real oscilloscope. Along the way you will hit the same problems every digital designer hits — a signal that glitches, a counter that free-runs, a testbench that lies to you — and learn to reason your way out of them.
That debugging instinct, more than any single lab, is the point.
Note to Students: These notes are intended solely for educational purposes. They are not a replacement for attending lectures or consulting textbooks, but rather a complementary resource to support your learning.

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
1.1 The digital design cycle
This first lab has two goals. First, to introduce the digital design cycle — the sequence of steps every digital circuit goes through, from an idea to a working bitstream on real hardware — so that you understand why each later lab does what it does. Second, to get your machine set up with the toolchain we use throughout the course, so the remaining labs are about designing hardware rather than fighting installers.
Every design in this course, however small, passes through the same stages:
Steps 3–7 are exactly what a toolchain automates for you. Knowing this sequence matters because when something goes wrong, the first useful question is which stage failed — a syntax error is a design-entry problem, a mismatch with the testbench is a verification problem, an unroutable design is a place & route problem, and an LED that doesn’t light despite a clean build is a hardware/pin-constraint problem. Each points you to a different fix.

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
Specification — describe, in plain language, what the circuit must do: its inputs, its outputs, and the relationship between them.
RTL design entry — write that behavior in a hardware description language. In this course, that language is SystemVerilog.
Functional verification (simulation) — before touching real hardware, simulate the design against a testbench to check it behaves as specified. Bugs are far cheaper to find here than on a board.
Synthesis — translate the RTL description into a gate-level netlist: a graph of primitive logic cells and the wires connecting them.
Place & route (implementation) — map that netlist onto the FPGA’s actual resources (logic cells, routing wires, I/O pins), respecting the timing and pin constraints you provide.
Bitstream generation — package the placed-and-routed design into the binary configuration file the FPGA fabric loads on power-up.
Programming — load the bitstream onto the physical board.
Hardware validation — check that the programmed board actually does what you specified in step 1. If it doesn’t, you go back to step 1 or 2 and iterate.

1.2 Tools used in this course
In previous years this course used Xilinx Vivado, a proprietary, vendor-specific design suite. Starting this year, we use Anvil — a small, open-source CLI that drives an entirely open FPGA flow (no license, no account, no multi-GB installer). Anvil orchestrates the same stages described above using open tools:



Design cycle stage
Tool




Design entry
SystemVerilog (you write top.sv)


Simulation
Icarus Verilog (iverilog) + GTKWave, via anvil test


Synthesis
sv2v (SystemVerilog → Verilog) feeding Yosys


Place & route
VPR (part of the F4PGA project — Yosys + VPR together)


Bitstream generation
F4PGA


Programming
openFPGALoader



Anvil itself just wires these tools together behind a handful of commands (anvil init, anvil build, anvil test, anvil program) so you don’t invoke each one by hand.
Anvil supports two FPGA boards, the Digilent Nexys A7 100T and the Nexys A7 50T. Both boards are used across the exercises in this course.






Nexys A7 50T



Anvil supports both the Nexys A7 100T and the Nexys A7 50T (support for the 50T was added in Anvil 1.1.0).
Your own computer: a normal installation works out of the box. If you installed Anvil before the 50T was added, run anvil update once.
Classroom computers: these have an older Anvil and you cannot run anvil update there (it needs sudo). Apply the classroom patch instead; it needs no administrator rights and changes only files in your home directory:
wget https://gist.githubusercontent.com/RatkoFri/d12d34610a58260a58a803eec74e7185/raw/anvil-nexys50t.sh
bash anvil-nexys50t.sh
source ~/.bashrc
Run it once per account; running it again does no harm. Check the result with anvil boards (both boards should be listed) and anvil doctor. Then start a 50T project with:
anvil init --board Nexys-A7-50T --example switches-leds

1.3 Installing Anvil
Prerequisites: a native Ubuntu 22.04 LTS machine, or WSL2 on Windows (the docs call out the handful of WSL-only steps, mainly around forwarding the board’s USB connection, as “WSL only”). Docker support is not available yet.
The recommended path is the automated setup script:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LogiSmith/toolchain-setup/main/install.sh | bash
If you’d rather review the script before running it (always a reasonable instinct when piping a script into a shell):
git clone https://github.com/LogiSmith/toolchain-setup.git
cd toolchain-setup
less install.sh
./install.sh
A successful run ends with a green ✓ Toolchain installed and all tests passed banner. Open a new shell afterward (so your updated PATH/aliases take effect) and verify with:
anvil doctor
For manual, tool-by-tool installation steps, WSL2-specific USB forwarding, and troubleshooting, see the full LogiSmith installation docs — that page is the canonical reference and is more likely to stay current than a copy pasted here.






Editor tip: SystemVerilog syntax highlighting and linting in VS Code



Plain .sv files have no syntax highlighting in VS Code out of the box. Install Verilog-HDL/SystemVerilog (publisher mshr-h) for SystemVerilog syntax highlighting and snippets, plus linting that reports syntax and elaboration errors directly in the editor as you type, instead of only after running anvil build or iverilog.
The extension needs to be pointed at a linter. Since this course already installs Icarus Verilog as part of the Anvil toolchain, set verilog.linting.linter to iverilog in the extension’s settings rather than installing a separate tool like Verilator or Verible just for this. The iverilog executable needs to be on your PATH, which the Anvil installer already takes care of.

title: 1  First exercise: Tools and the Digital Design Cycle
text:
1.4 Your first design: basic_comb
With anvil doctor passing, build a first design that exercises switches and LEDs directly, with no clock involved: a small combinational circuit.
mkdir basic_comb && cd basic_comb
anvil init --board Nexys-A7-100T
This scaffolds a project:
basic_comb/
├── config.json    # board + module configuration
├── top.sv         # top-level design — edit this
├── *.xdc          # pin constraints, copied from the board master
├── tb/            # testbenches
└── Makefile

1.4.0.1 What’s in config.json
config.json is the per-project manifest every anvil command reads (build, test, program). anvil init --board Nexys-A7-100T fills it in for you, so you won’t normally hand-edit it in this lab — but it’s worth knowing what’s there:
{
  "project": "basic_comb",
  "board": "Nexys-A7-100T",
  "top": "top",
  "target": "nexys4ddr",
  "partname": "xc7a100tcsg324-1",
  "device": "artix7",
  "ofl_board": "nexys_a7_100",
  "xdc": "Nexys-A7-100T-Master.xdc"
}

project — the project’s name, defaulting to the directory name.
board — which entry of Anvil’s board registry (boards.json) this project targets; everything below top is copied in from that registry at anvil init time.
top — the top-level module name Anvil looks for when it builds your design. It defaults to top, which is exactly why the module in top.sv needs to be named top rather than basic_comb.
partname, device, target, ofl_board, xdc — board-specific details (exact FPGA part, device family, Makefile build target, openFPGALoader board identifier, and master constraints filename) that synthesis, place & route, and programming each need. You won’t touch these directly for the Nexys A7 100T.
modules (not shown above, since this design has none) — a list of reusable RTL module dependencies with pinned versions, e.g. "uart@1.0.0", added automatically by anvil addmodule. You’ll meet this once a later lab pulls in a shared peripheral block.

Replace the contents of top.sv with three switch inputs feeding four LED outputs through simple boolean logic. Anvil expects the top-level module in top.sv to be named top, so the logic below is the same as the basic_comb.sv starter file, just renamed from basic_comb to top:
// basic_comb — simple 3-input combinational logic
module top (
    input  logic a,        // SW0
    input  logic b,        // SW1
    input  logic c,        // SW2
    output logic [3:0] y   // LED0–LED3
);
    assign y[0] = a & b | c;
    assign y[1] = a & c;
    assign y[2] = a | c;
    assign y[3] = a & b & c;
endmodule


1.4.0.2 Explanation

Continuous assignment: each assign statement drives its output from a boolean expression of the inputs, re-evaluated any time a, b, or c changes. There is no clock and no memory — the outputs are a pure function of the current switch positions, which is exactly what “combinational logic” means.
This is the design-entry stage: assign is the idiomatic way to describe combinational logic in SystemVerilog, the same way always_ff (which you’ll meet in the next lab) is the idiom for sequential logic.
Four independent outputs: y[0]–y[3] are four separate circuits sharing the same three inputs — nothing requires a module to have only one output bit.

Uncomment (or check) the pins for a, b, c, and y in the generated .xdc file — they should look like this:
set_property PACKAGE_PIN J15 [get_ports {a}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {a}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN L16 [get_ports {b}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {b}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN M13 [get_ports {c}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {c}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN H17 [get_ports {y[0]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[0]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN K15 [get_ports {y[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[1]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN J13 [get_ports {y[2]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[2]}]

set_property PACKAGE_PIN N14 [get_ports {y[3]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {y[3]}]
This maps a, b, c to switches SW0–SW2 and y[0]–y[3] to LED0–LED3 on the Nexys A7 100T. Unlike Blinky, there’s no create_clock line here — a purely combinational design has no clock port for the timing analyzer to check.
Then build and program the board:
anvil build       # sv2v → Yosys → VPR → bitstream, a few seconds
anvil program     # flash the bitstream to the board via openFPGALoader
If everything worked, flipping SW0–SW2 should change the LED0–LED3 pattern according to the four equations above.

text:
2.2 Module
All system modules in Verilog are encapsulated inside a module. Modules can include instantiation of lower-level modules to support hierarchical designs. The keywords module and endmodule mark the beginning and the end of the system description.
module ModuleName(
    portType signalType Port1_name,
    portType signalType Port2_name, Port3_name,
    .......
    portType signalType PortN_name
);
where the portType specifies the direction of the port (input, output, or inout), and signalType defines the type of the signal, as described in the previous section.







Port Type
Description




input
Specifies an input port to the module. Data flows into the module through this port.


output
Specifies an output port from the module. Data flows out of the module through this port.


inout
Specifies a bidirectional port. Data can flow both into and out of the module through this port.

text:
2.4 Modeling Concurent functionality in SystemVerilog

2.4.1 Continuous assignment
Continuous assignment in SystemVerilog allows for the assignment of values to nets using the assign keyword, ensuring that the assigned value is continuously updated whenever the right-hand side expression changes. A continuous assignment models combinational logic. For example:
assign out = a & b; // 'out' is continuously assigned the result of 'a & b'
We need to differ continous assignment from assignment in programming languages.
First example:
assign b = a; 
assign c = b;
In programming languages, a similar construct will first assign the value of a to b, and then pass the value of b to c. During synthesis, the tool will remove signal b and infer assign c = a.
Second example:
assign c = a; 
assign c = b;
In programming languages, a similar construct will first assign the value of a to c, and then assign the value of b to c. The final value of c will be determined by the last assignment. During synthesis, the tool will create a net driven by two signals. As these signals by have different values, the net c will have an unknown value X. This situation must be avoided at all costs.


2.4.2 4-bit 4:1 Multiplexer
The 4-bit multiplexer (MUX) selects one of the four 4-bit inputs to pass to the output based on the 2-bit selection signal.
module mux4to1 (
    input logic [3:0] in0, // 4-bit input 0
    input logic [3:0] in1, // 4-bit input 1
    input logic [3:0] in2, // 4-bit input 2
    input logic [3:0] in3, // 4-bit input 3
    input logic [1:0] sel, // 2-bit selection signal
    output logic [3:0] out // 4-bit output
);
    // Nested conditional operator 
    // C = (A > B) ? 1 : (A < B) ? 0 : 1 
    assign out = (sel == 2'b00) ? in0 :
                 (sel == 2'b01) ? in1 :
                 (sel == 2'b10) ? in2 :
                 (sel == 2'b11) ? in3 :
                 4'b0000; // Default case 

endmodule

2.4.2.1 Explanation

Module Declaration: The module mux4to1 is declared with inputs and outputs.
Inputs: Four 4-bit inputs (in0, in1, in2, in3) and a 2-bit selection signal (sel).
Output: One 4-bit output (out).
Conditional Statement: The assign statement uses a series of conditional (ternary) operators to select one of the four inputs based on the value of the 2-bit selection signal (sel).




2.4.3 4-bit adder
The 4-bit adder adds two 4-bit binary numbers and produces a 4-bit sum and a carry-out bit.
module adder4bit (
    input logic [3:0] a, // 4-bit input a
    input logic [3:0] b, // 4-bit input b
    output logic [3:0] sum, // 4-bit sum output
    output logic carry_out // Carry-out bit
);

    logic c1, c2, c3; // Intermediate carry bits

    // Half Adder for the least significant bit
    assign sum[0] = a[0] ^ b[0];
    assign c1 = a[0] & b[0];

    // Full Adder for the second bit
    assign sum[1] = a[1] ^ b[1] ^ c1;
    assign c2 = (a[1] & b[1]) | (c1 & (a[1] ^ b[1]));

    // Full Adder for the third bit
    assign sum[2] = a[2] ^ b[2] ^ c2;
    assign c3 = (a[2] & b[2]) | (c2 & (a[2] ^ b[2]));

    // Full Adder for the most significant bit
    assign sum[3] = a[3] ^ b[3] ^ c3;
    assign carry_out = (a[3] & b[3]) | (c3 & (a[3] ^ b[3]));

endmodule

2.4.3.1 Explanation

Module Declaration: The module adder4bit is declared with two 4-bit inputs (a and b), a 4-bit output (sum), and a carry-out bit (carry_out).
Intermediate Carry Bits: Three intermediate carry bits (c1, c2, c3) are used to store the carry from each adder stage.
Half Adder: The least significant bit is added using a half adder, which produces the sum and the first carry bit (c1).
Full Adders: The next three bits are added using full adders, which take into account the carry from the previous stage.
Final Carry-Out: The carry-out from the most significant bit is assigned to carry_out.




2.4.4 User Constraints Files and Pin Planning in Vivado
In Vivado, User Constraints Files (UCF) or Xilinx Design Constraints (XDC) files are used to define the physical constraints of the design, such as pin assignments, timing constraints, and other implementation-specific parameters. Pin planning involves mapping the logical signals in your design to the physical pins on the FPGA. This process ensures that the design interfaces correctly with external components and meets the required performance criteria. Proper pin planning and constraint management are crucial for successful FPGA implementation, as they directly impact signal integrity, timing closure, and overall design functionality.
The XDC file for Nexys A7 defines the pin placement for external signals of modules. To map the inputs of our adder4bit to the switches and the outputs to LEDs, we need to make the following changes:
##Switches
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[0] }]; #IO_L24N_T3_RS0_15 Sch=sw[0]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN L16   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[1] }]; #IO_L3N_T0_DQS_EMCCLK_14 Sch=sw[1]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN M13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[2] }]; #IO_L6N_T0_D08_VREF_14 Sch=sw[2]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { a[3] }]; #IO_L13N_T2_MRCC_14 Sch=sw[3]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[0] }]; #IO_L12N_T1_MRCC_14 Sch=sw[4]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN T18   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[1] }]; #IO_L7N_T1_D10_14 Sch=sw[5]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN U18   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[2] }]; #IO_L17N_T2_A13_D29_14 Sch=sw[6]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { b[3] }]; #IO_L5N_T0_D07_14 Sch=sw[7]

##LEDS
## LEDs
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN H17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[0] }]; #IO_L18P_T2_A24_15 Sch=led[0]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN K15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[1] }]; #IO_L24P_T3_RS1_15 Sch=led[1]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[2] }]; #IO_L17N_T2_A25_15 Sch=led[2]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN N14   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { sum[3] }]; #IO_L8P_T1_D11_14 Sch=led[3]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN R18   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { carry_out }]; #IO_L7P_T1_D09_14 Sch=led[4]
It is important to assign the appropriate pin to the get_ports function.

2.5 Assignment
Your task is to implement a “dummy” 4-bit Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) with the following interface: - a, b: 4-bit inputs - alu_control: 3-bit input for selecting the operation - c: 4-bit output



alu_control Value
Operation




000
Addition

Subtraction


010
Bitwise AND


011
Bitwise OR


100

101
Compare (equal)


110
Pass-through b


111
Pass-through a









Note



The ALU is 4-bit rather than 6-bit specifically to keep addition/subtraction small. The open-source Artix-7 flow (F4PGA: Yosys + VPR) that Anvil uses has known weak spots mapping inferred carry-chain arithmetic (+/-) — the same CARRY4 logic behind the adder4bit example above — and wider inferred adders can blow up synthesis time and resource usage. Staying at 4 bits, matching adder4bit’s width, keeps you well clear of that.


Tips: 1. Employ operators and intermediate signals to obtain the results of each operation. 2. Connect input signals to the rightmost switches (SW0 to SW7), and selection signals to the leftmost switches (SW13 to SW15). The output signal should be connected to LEDs (LED0 to LED3). 3. Employ nested conditionals.

3.1 Designing D Flip-Flop in SystemVerilog
Vivado recognizes certain idioms and transforms them into specific sequential circuits. Other coding styles may simulate correctly but may synthesize into circuits with obvious or subtle errors. We will present the proper idioms to describe registers and latches.
The Verilog code for a D flip-flop (DFF) active on the positive clock edge with a synchronous reset is given below:
The always_ff has it roots from Verilog language. In Verilog we have always statement, written in form:
In the previous code, the statement is executed only when the event specified in the sensitivity list occurs. For the D-FF example, the event is posedge clk, meaning the statements inside always_ff will execute on the positive edge of the clock. Inside the always_ff block, we use an if/else statement for conditional operations. Notice that the non-blocking operator <= is used inside the always_ff block. On every positive edge of the clock, the block checks if the reset is active. If the reset is active, the output will be set to zero; otherwise, the input will be copied to the output. The always_ff construct behaves like the always construct but is specifically used to imply flip-flops and allows tools to produce a warning if anything else is implied.
Let us design 4-bit counter, which counts on positive edge and has active high reset
As in the previous example, every time posedge clk occurs, the counter will increment the value of the internal counter counter if reset is low. Otherwise, the counter will start counting from zero. Finally, we output the state of the internal counter to the output. Note that assign and always_ff work in parallel.

3.4 Task: Implement a 4-bit Gray Code Counter
Your task is to implement a 4-bit Gray Code counter, that changes its state with the frequency of 1 Hz.
Steps required: 1. Start with two counters: a modulo 10010^6 counter and a classical binary counter that counts from 0 to 15. 2. The first counter increments its value every system clock cycle. 3. The other counter changes its value when the first counter reaches the value 10010^6-1. When the input up_down is equal to 0, the counter increments its value; otherwise it decreases. 4. Convert the state of the binary counter to Gray Code.
Python code snippet that illustrates the behaviour of gray code counter
binary_count = 0;

while(1):
    for i in range (0, 100 * 1e6): # the module 100*1e6 counter 
        if(i==100 * 1e6-1):
            if(up_down==0):
                binary_count = binary_count + 1
            else:
                binary_count = binary_count - 1
    
    gray_code = bin2gray(binary_count )
def bin2gray(binary):

        case 0: return 0
        case 1: return 1
        case 2: return 3
        case 3: return 2
        case 4: return 6
        case 5: return 7
        case 6: return 5
        case 7: return 4
        case 8: return 12
        case 9: return 13
        case 10: return 15
        case 11: return 14
        case 12: return 10
        case 13: return 11
        case 14: return 9
        case 15: return 8
        case _: return 0

text:
3.5 Implementation guidelines
Structural modeling, splitting a design into separate modules and instantiating them, is introduced in the next exercise. For now gray_code_counter stays a single module, so the three pieces below are not separate modules with their own ports, but three cooperating pieces of behavioral code inside gray_code_counter, sharing the internal signals en and binary_count already declared in the skeleton above. These three pieces of code are actually three separate always blocks, where first two are always_ff and the last one is always_comb. The first two blocks are sequential, the last one is combinational. The three pieces are described below.

3.5.1 Divider
The divider turns the 100 MHz system clock into a single, once-per-second pulse on en. It is a free running counter, the same idea you will meet again as the standalone prescaler module in the next exercise.
Declare an internal register wide enough to count up to 100,000,000:
logic [26:0] div_count; // 2^27 > 100,000,000
Behavior:

On every rising edge of clk, if rst is high, reset div_count to zero.
Otherwise, increment div_count by one on every rising edge. This is step 2 from above, the first counter incrementing every system clock cycle.
When div_count reaches 100,000,000 - 1, drive en high for that clock cycle and let div_count wrap back to zero on the next edge, restarting the count.
The result is a single clock cycle pulse on en once every 100,000,000 clock cycles. At 100 MHz that is exactly once per second.



3.5.2 Up/down binary counter
binary_count is the 4-bit counter whose value eventually gets Gray encoded for the LEDs. Unlike div_count, it does not advance on every clock edge. It only advances once per second, on a clock edge where en is high.
Behavior:

On every rising edge of clk, if rst is high, reset binary_count to zero.
Otherwise, only change binary_count on a clock edge where en is high. When up_down is 0, increment binary_count, wrapping from 15 back to 0. When up_down is 1, decrement it, wrapping from 0 back to 15.
On a clock edge where en is low, hold binary_count at its current value.
Because en pulses only once per second, binary_count also only changes once per second, which is where the counter’s 1 Hz update rate comes from.



3.5.3 Gray code converter
The converter has no state of its own. It is a purely combinational function of binary_count, mapping each of the 16 possible values to the corresponding Gray code word from the bin2gray table above.
Behavior:

Use always_comb with a case statement on binary_count, one branch per value 0 through 15, assigning the matching Gray code word to gray_code in each branch.
Always include a default branch, even though cases 0 through 15 already cover every possible 4-bit value. The Common mistakes section earlier in this chapter explains why an incomplete case without a default infers a latch instead of the combinational logic you intended.
Because the conversion is combinational, gray_code updates immediately whenever binary_count changes. No separate clocking is needed here. binary_count already only changes once per second, so gray_code will too.



3.5.4 Pin mapping
Connect the clk signal to the system clock (100 MHz), the rst signal to the middle button, the up_down signal to the switch, and the gray_code signal to the LEDs.
## Clock signal
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN E3    IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { clk }]; #IO_L12P_T1_MRCC_35 Sch=clk100mhz
create_clock -add -name sys_clk_pin -period 10.00 -waveform {0 5} [get_ports {clk}];


##Switches
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { up_down }]; #IO_L24N_T3_RS0_15 Sch=sw[0]

## LEDs
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN H17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[0] }]; #IO_L18P_T2_A24_15 Sch=led[0]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN K15   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[1] }]; #IO_L24P_T3_RS1_15 Sch=led[1]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J13   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[2] }]; #IO_L17N_T2_A25_15 Sch=led[2]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN N14   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { gray_code[3] }]; #IO_L8P_T1_D11_14 Sch=led[3]

##Buttons
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN N17   IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { rst }]; #IO_L9P_T1_DQS_14 Sch=btnc

4.1 Parametrized components
In the previous exercise, we focused on designing counters or flip-flops by describing their functionality in SystemVerilog. This style of modeling is referred to as behavioral modeling. This exercise focuses on structural modeling, where we describe a module in terms of how it is composed of simpler modules. In the example below, we assemble a 4:1 multiplexer from three 2:1 multiplexers. Each copy of the 2:1 multiplexer is called an instance and has a unique name.
As we can see, the instantiation of a module has following syntax: first, we specify the module name, followed by the instance name. In parentheses, we connect the module’s inputs and outputs to signals defined at the current level of hierarchy.

4.3 Task: Implement a PWM (Pulse-Width Modulation) module for RGB LED
In this task, you will implement a PWM module for an RGB LED. The module will have three 6-bit inputs, each controlling the duty cycle of the red, green, and blue LEDs. The module will have three 1-bit outputs, each representing the PWM signal for the red, green, and blue LEDs.
The PWM signal will be generated by comparing the duty cycle with a 4-bit counter that increments with the PWM_tick signal. The PWM_tick signal is generated by a prescaler that outputs a pulse every 3125 clock cycles, corresponding to a frequency of 32 kHz. You will connect the PWM module to the prescaler and the RGB LED module according to the diagram below.


Note: The N16, R11, and G14 pins on the FPGA board are connected to the red, green, and blue LEDs of the RGB LED, respectively.

Switch values denote duty cycle for each color. The duty cycle is calculated as follows:



SW[1:0]
Duty_cycle

0 %


01
12.5 %


10
25 %


11
50 %



Duty cycle is definied as ratio of high signal to the period of the signal, e.g. 25% duty cycle means that the signal is high for 25% of the period.

4.3.1 PWM time diagram



4.3.2 Extension: oscilloscope probe
An LED only tells you the PWM signal’s average brightness. To actually see the waveform, duty cycle, and period on an oscilloscope, add two more switches, SW[7:6], that select which of the three RGB PWM signals gets mirrored onto a new single-bit output port, pwm_out. Wire pwm_out to a Pmod header pin so you can clip a scope probe onto it. For connecting the probe and reading the signal once it’s wired up, see the oscilloscope appendix.

text:
4.4 Implementation guidelines

4.4.1 Prescaler
The prescaler turns the fast system clock into the slower pwm_tick the PWM module counts on. It is a free running counter that produces a single cycle pulse once every limit clock cycles. Its interface is already declared in the starter file:
module prescaler
    #(parameter PRESCALER_WIDTH = 8)
    (
        input logic clk,
        input logic rst,
        input logic [PRESCALER_WIDTH-1:0] limit,
        output logic pwm_tick
    );









Port
Direction
Width
Description




clk
input
1 bit
System clock. The counter advances on its rising edge.


rst
input
1 bit
Synchronous reset. Clears the internal counter while high.


limit
input
PRESCALER_WIDTH bits
Number of clock cycles between output pulses.


pwm_tick
output
1 bit
Pulses high for one clock cycle, once every limit cycles.



Behavior:

Keep an internal counter register. On every rising edge of clk, if rst is high, reset that counter to zero.
Otherwise, increment the counter by one on every rising edge.
When the counter reaches limit - 1, drive pwm_tick high for that clock cycle and let the counter wrap back to zero on the next edge, restarting the count.
The result is a periodic, single cycle pulse with a period of exactly limit clock cycles. With limit = 3125 and a 100 MHz clk, pwm_tick fires once every 31.25 microseconds, which is 32 kHz.



4.4.2 PWM controller
The PWM controller turns a 2-bit duty cycle selection into a single PWM output for one LED color. One instance drives the red LED, one drives green, one drives blue, each fed by its own pair of switches and all three sharing the same pwm_tick from the prescaler. Its interface is already declared in the starter file:
module PWM_controller
(
    input logic clk,
    input logic rst,
    input logic [1:0] SW,
    input logic pwm_tick,
    output logic PWM
);









Port
Direction
Width
Description




clk
input
1 bit
System clock, used to advance the internal counter register.


rst
input
1 bit
Synchronous reset. Clears the internal counter while high.


SW
input
2 bits
Duty cycle selector for this color, per the duty cycle table above.


pwm_tick
input
1 bit
One clock cycle pulse from the prescaler. Acts as a count enable.


PWM
output
1 bit
The pulse width modulated signal driving one RGB LED color.



Behavior:

Keep an internal 4-bit counter register. Unlike the prescaler, this counter does not advance on every clk edge. It advances by one only on a clk edge where pwm_tick is high, and wraps from 15 back to 0. Sixteen pwm_tick pulses therefore make up one full PWM period.
On a clk edge where rst is high, reset that counter to zero instead of counting.
Translate SW into a threshold on the same 0 to 15 scale as the counter, so it lines up with the duty cycle table: 00 maps to a threshold of 0, 01 to 2, 10 to 4, and 11 to 8 (0, 2, 4, and 8 sixteenths are 0%, 12.5%, 25%, and 50%).
Drive PWM combinationally from the comparison: high while the counter value is less than the threshold, low otherwise. Since the counter counts through all 16 values once per period, this produces a high pulse whose width, as a fraction of the period, equals the selected duty cycle.



4.4.3 Top level: rgb_controller
The top module has no logic of its own beyond the oscilloscope channel selector described below. It otherwise only wires the prescaler and three PWM_controller instances together, using structural modeling exactly as introduced at the start of this chapter. Its interface, extended with the oscilloscope probe from the task above, is already declared in the starter file:
module rgb_controller (
    input logic clock,
    input logic reset,
    input logic [7:0] SW,
    output logic [2:0] RGB,
    output logic pwm_out
);









Port
Direction
Width
Description




clock
input
1 bit
System clock (100 MHz), forwarded to every instance below.


reset
input
1 bit
Synchronous reset, forwarded to every instance below.


SW
input
8 bits
SW[5:0]: duty cycle selectors, two bits per color (SW[1:0] red, SW[3:2] green, SW[5:4] blue). SW[7:6]: oscilloscope channel select.


RGB
output
3 bits
One PWM signal per color: RGB[0] red, RGB[1] green, RGB[2] blue.


pwm_out
output
1 bit
Mirrors whichever RGB bit SW[7:6] selects, for probing with an oscilloscope.



Structure:

One instance of prescaler, driven by clock/reset and the limit_value already wired up in the draft, produces a single pwm_tick signal shared by everything downstream.
Three instances of PWM_controller, conventionally named PWM_red, PWM_green, and PWM_blue. These are three separate instances of the exact same module, the same way mux2to1 was instantiated three times to build mux4to1 earlier in this chapter, not three different modules. Each instance shares clock, reset, and the one pwm_tick from the prescaler, but connects to a different 2-bit slice of SW and drives a different bit of RGB. For example, the red instance looks like:

PWM_controller PWM_red (
    .clk(clock),
    .rst(reset),
    .SW(SW[1:0]),
    .pwm_tick(pwm_tick),
    .PWM(RGB[0])
);
PWM_green and PWM_blue follow the same pattern, connecting SW[3:2]/RGB[1] and SW[5:4]/RGB[2] respectively. The draft file’s instantiation comments all read “for the red LED”. That’s a leftover from copy-pasting the first instance, and should read green and blue for the other two.

On top of the three instances above, drive pwm_out from RGB with a combinational multiplexer on SW[7:6], using always_comb and case exactly as introduced for Mux4to1 in the previous exercise:

always_comb begin
    case (SW[7:6])
        2'b00: pwm_out = RGB[0];
        2'b01: pwm_out = RGB[1];
        2'b10: pwm_out = RGB[2];
        default: pwm_out = 1'b0;
    endcase
end
SW[7:6] = 2'b11 has no explicit case, so it falls through to default, holding pwm_out at 1'b0 rather than leaving it undriven. Always keep that default branch, even on cases that look fully covered. Leaving it out, as the “Infering latch” mistake earlier in the previous chapter explains, would infer a latch instead of the combinational multiplexer you want.

Create a testbench to verify the functionality of your PWM module. The testbench is provided in the repository.



4.4.4 Testbenches for prescaler and PWM_controller
Before wiring everything together, verify prescaler and PWM_controller on their own, the same way tb_mux4to1 and tb_counter tested individual modules earlier in this chapter. A bug isolated to one small module is far easier to find than the same bug hiding inside the fully assembled rgb_controller.

4.4.4.1 tb_prescaler
module tb_prescaler;

    // Testbench signals
    logic clk;
    logic rst;
    logic [7:0] limit;
    logic pwm_tick;

    // Instantiate the DUT
    prescaler dut (
        .clk(clk),
        .rst(rst),
        .limit(limit),
        .pwm_tick(pwm_tick)
    );

    // Clock generation
    always begin
        #5 clk = ~clk; // Toggle clock every 5 time units
    end

    // Test procedure
    initial begin
        $dumpfile("tb_prescaler.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, tb_prescaler);

        clk = 0;
        rst = 1;
        limit = 5;
        #10;
        rst = 0;

        // Let the counter run through several periods
        #200;

        $finish;
    end

    // Log every pwm_tick pulse
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (pwm_tick)
            $display("t=%0t pwm_tick pulse", $time);
    end

endmodule






Note



Do not test with limit = 3125, the value you will eventually use on hardware. At 100 MHz that is a pulse every 31.25 microseconds, so watching even a handful of periods in simulation means sitting through thousands of clock cycles of $display output or a huge waveform. Drive limit with a small value instead, such as 5 as above, so pwm_tick fires every few clock cycles and you can see several full periods and the counter wraparound in a short simulation run. Once the counting and wraparound logic is confirmed correct at a small limit, the same logic is correct at limit = 3125, only slower.




4.4.4.2 tb_pwm_controller
PWM_controller takes pwm_tick as an input rather than generating it, so this testbench stands in for the prescaler with a small free running counter of its own, pulsing pwm_tick high for one clock cycle out of every 4, instead of instantiating a full prescaler with a large limit. The DUT’s internal counter then advances once every 4 clock cycles, so a full 16-step PWM period takes 64 clock cycles to simulate, still far shorter than testing against the real limit = 3125 prescaler.
module tb_pwm_controller;

    // Testbench signals
    logic clk;
    logic rst;
    logic [1:0] SW;
    logic pwm_tick;
    logic PWM;

    // Instantiate the DUT
    PWM_controller dut (
        .clk(clk),
        .rst(rst),
        .SW(SW),
        .pwm_tick(pwm_tick),
        .PWM(PWM)
    );

    // Clock generation
    always begin
        #5 clk = ~clk; // Toggle clock every 5 time units
    end

    // Stand in for the prescaler: pulse pwm_tick high for one cycle
    // out of every 4 clock cycles
    logic [1:0] tick_count;

    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        tick_count <= tick_count + 1;
    end

    assign pwm_tick = (tick_count == 2'd3);

    // Test procedure
    initial begin
        $dumpfile("tb_pwm_controller.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, tb_pwm_controller);

        clk = 0;
        rst = 1;
        tick_count = 0;
        SW = 2'b00;
        #10;
        rst = 0;

        // Run two full 64-cycle periods (1280 time units) at each duty cycle
        SW = 2'b00; #1280;   // 0 %
        SW = 2'b01; #1280;   // 12.5 %
        SW = 2'b10; #1280;   // 25 %
        SW = 2'b11; #1280;   // 50 %

        $finish;
    end

    // Log every PWM transition, so you can measure how long it stays
    // high relative to the 16-cycle period for each SW value
    always @(PWM) begin
        $display("t=%0t SW=%b PWM=%b", $time, SW, PWM);
    end

endmodule
Both testbenches call $dumpfile/$dumpvars up front, so running them through anvil test or iverilog/vvp produces a .vcd file you can open with gtkwave tb_prescaler.vcd & or gtkwave tb_pwm_controller.vcd &, as described earlier in this chapter. Watching pwm_tick and the internal counters directly in the waveform is often faster than reading through $display output.



4.4.5 Pin mapping
Connect the clock signal to the system clock (100 MHz), the reset signal to the middle button, switches SW[5:0] to the duty-cycle inputs (two bits per color), switches SW[7:6] to the oscilloscope channel select, the three RGB[2:0] outputs to the RGB LED, and pwm_out to a Pmod header pin for the scope probe. Add these to the project’s .xdc file, following the same set_property PACKAGE_PIN / set_property IOSTANDARD pattern used in the tools intro:

text:
5.1 Seven segment display
A seven-segment display is an electronic display device used to show decimal digits and some letters. It consists of seven bar-shaped LEDs arranged in a figure eight. Each LED is called a segment because, when lit, it forms one part of the character being displayed. Most displays also include an eighth LED, the decimal point (DP), in the lower right corner.
As Figure 5.1 shows, segment A sits at the top and the labels run clockwise through B, C, D, E and F. Segment G is the middle bar. Lighting different combinations of segments produces the digits 0 to 9 and the hexadecimal letters A to F. For example, the digit 1 lights only B and C, while the digit 8 lights all seven segments.
crumbs: 5  Fifth exercise: Counter and seven segment display

title: 5  Fifth exercise: Counter and seven segment display
text:
Figure 5.1: Segment layout of a seven-segment display. Segments are labeled A to G clockwise from the top, with G in the middle. DP is the decimal point.





5.1.1 Common anode vs common cathode configuration
Each segment is an LED, and an LED lights up only when current flows from its anode (positive terminal) to its cathode (negative terminal). To save pins, the eight LEDs of one digit share a common terminal. Which terminal they share determines the logic level that turns a segment on.

Common anode (CA). All anodes are tied together and held at logic 1. Each cathode has its own control signal. Driving a cathode to logic 0 lets current flow, so the segment lights. Driving it to logic 1 leaves both terminals at the same level, so the segment stays dark. The segments are therefore active low.
Common cathode (CC). All cathodes are tied together and held at logic 0. Each anode has its own control signal. Driving an anode to logic 1 lights the segment, and driving it to logic 0 turns it off. The segments are therefore active high.










Configuration
Common terminal
Segment on
Segment off




Common anode (CA)
Anodes at logic 1
Cathode at logic 0
Cathode at logic 1


Common cathode (CC)
Cathodes at logic 0
Anode at logic 1
Anode at logic 0



The Nexys A7 uses common anode displays. Keep this in mind when you write the segment patterns: a segment that should be lit needs a 0 in your code, not a 1.


5.1.2 Nexys A7 and seven-segment display
The Nexys A7 has eight common anode seven-segment digits. They are wired to the FPGA with two groups of signals:

Cathodes CA to CG (and DP). These are shared by all eight digits. Segment CA on digit 0 is wired to segment CA on every other digit. A cathode at logic 0 lights its segment.
Anodes AN0 to AN7. Each digit has its own anode signal, which switches that digit on or off. An anode at logic 0 turns its digit on.


Note: You might expect the anode signals to be active high, since they drive the common anode. On the board, however, each ANx signal controls a transistor that switches the supply to its digit. That transistor conducts when ANx is at logic 0. So both the anodes and the cathodes are active low. See Figure 9.1 in the Nexys A7 reference manual.

The board has only one set of cathode signals, so at any moment all enabled digits show the same pattern. To display eight different digits, the design uses time multiplexing. It enables one digit at a time and puts that digit’s pattern on the shared cathodes. Then it moves on to the next digit, and so on in a continuous loop:

Set AN0 to logic 0 and all other anodes to logic 1. Drive the cathodes with the pattern for digit 0. Only digit 0 lights.
After a short time, set AN1 to logic 0 and the rest to logic 1. Drive the cathodes with the pattern for digit 1. Only digit 1 lights.
Continue the same way up to AN7, then start again at AN0.







Figure 5.2: Time multiplexing the eight digits. Exactly one anode is at logic 0 in each 2 ms slot, while the shared cathodes CA to CG carry that digit’s pattern.



Figure 5.2 shows the timing used in this lab. Each digit is on for a digit period of 2 ms, so one pass over all eight digits takes a refresh period of 8 × 2 ms = 16 ms. Each digit is lit only one eighth of the time. It still looks steady because of persistence of vision: when the refresh rate is above roughly 60 Hz, the eye cannot see the flicker. Here the refresh rate is 1 / 16 ms = 62.5 Hz. If the digit period is too long, the display visibly flickers. If it is too short, the digits look dim and can bleed into each other, because the LEDs do not have time to switch fully. The reference manual recommends a refresh period between 1 ms and 16 ms.

text:
5.2 Assignment
In this assignment you will build a seconds counter on the Nexys A7. The counter value appears on all eight seven-segment digits as a hexadecimal number. Switch SW0 starts and stops counting, and the centre button BTNC resets the counter to zero.

5.2.1 Design overview
The design has two levels of hierarchy. Figure 5.3 shows the top level. counter_1s produces a 32-bit count that increases once per second. SevSegDisplay splits that count into eight 4-bit hex digits and drives the display with time multiplexing.






Figure 5.3: Top-level design. The 32-bit count is split into eight nibbles, one per display digit.



Figure 5.4 shows what is inside SevSegDisplay. timer_002s produces a tick every 2 ms. On each tick, anode_assert moves to the next digit by driving one anode low. value_to_digit uses the same anode pattern to pick the matching nibble of the count. digit_to_segments turns that nibble into the cathode pattern.






Figure 5.4: Inside SevSegDisplay. The anode pattern from anode_assert both drives the display and selects which nibble is shown.



Build the design bottom up. Write each small module first and check it in simulation, then connect the modules together. All module skeletons are in the starter file top_draft.sv.


5.2.2 Step 1: Create the project
Create a new Anvil project for the Nexys A7 100T, as in the tools intro:
mkdir counter_7seg && cd counter_7seg
anvil init --board Nexys-A7-100T
Replace the contents of top.sv with the contents of top_draft.sv. It contains empty skeletons of every module in this assignment. You will fill them in during the following steps.


5.2.3 Step 2: timer_002s
This module produces a time_tick pulse that is high for exactly one clock cycle every 2 ms. It sets the digit period from Figure 5.2.
module timer_002s
    (
        input logic clock,
        input logic reset,
        output logic time_tick
    );
endmodule

Work out how many clock cycles fit in 2 ms. The clock runs at 100 MHz, so one cycle is 10 ns and 2 ms is 2 ms / 10 ns = 200 000 cycles.
Declare a counter register wide enough to hold 199 999. That needs 18 bits, because 2^18 = 262 144.
In an always_ff block, reset the counter to 0 when reset is high. Otherwise, increment it on every clock edge. When it reaches 199 999, wrap it back to 0.
Drive time_tick high only while the counter equals 199 999. This gives one pulse per 200 000 cycles.

This is the same idea as the prescaler from the previous exercise. A good alternative is to write one parametrized timer, timer #(parameter LIMIT = 200_000), and use it in both this step and the next. That also makes simulation easier, as Step 9 explains.


5.2.4 Step 3: counter_1s
This module holds the 32-bit count. The count increases by one every second while enable is high, and holds its value while enable is low.
module counter_1s
    (
        input logic clock,
        input logic reset,
        input logic enable,
        output logic [31:0] count
    );
endmodule

Inside the module, build a 1 s tick in the same way as in Step 2. One second is 100 000 000 cycles, so the prescaler counts from 0 to 99 999 999. That needs 27 bits.
Add a second register for count. Reset it to 0 when reset is high.
Increment count only on clock cycles where the 1 s tick is high and enable is high. On all other cycles, keep the old value.

Increment count on the system clock and use the tick as a condition. Do not use the tick as a clock. All flip-flops in the design should share the 100 MHz clock.

This module selects which digit is active. It has a 3-bit counter that advances on every 2 ms tick and turns the counter value into an active-low anode pattern.

    input logic reset,
    input logic clock_enable,       // time_tick from timer_002s
    output logic [7:0] anode_select

endmodule

Instantiate counter_1s and connect clock, reset, enable and count.

5.2.10 Step 9: Simulate
Simulate before you build. Finding a bug in GTKWave takes minutes. Finding it on the board takes much longer.
With the real limits, one second of hardware time is 100 million clock cycles, which is far too slow to simulate. Temporarily shrink the limits instead. For example, make the 2 ms timer tick every 4 cycles and the 1 s timer every 64 cycles. A parametrized timer from Step 2 makes this a one-line change. Remember to restore the real values before you build.
Use top_tb.sv as a starting point. Put it in the project’s tb/ folder and run it:

gtkwave tb/top_tb.vcd &

segs shows the correct pattern for the nibble selected by each anode value.
count increases only while enable is high, and returns to 0 when reset is pressed.

Check that the timer limits are back at their real values (200 000 and 100 000 000). Then build and program the board:

If the display looks wrong, use these hints:

All segments lit, or the digits look like garbled 8s: the segment patterns are probably inverted. Remember that a lit segment needs a 0.

title: 6  Sixth exercise: UART transmitter
text:
6.1 UART basics
So far the board could only talk to you through LEDs and the seven-segment display. In this exercise you will give it a voice. You will build a UART transmitter and use it to send the text Hello World! from the FPGA to a terminal on your computer, over the same USB cable you use to program the board.
UART is the simplest serial interface there is, and it is everywhere: microcontroller debug consoles, GPS modules, Bluetooth modules, and the console of the HIPV SoC you will meet later in the course. The HIPV SoC prints its messages through a UART peripheral that contains the same building blocks you write here. This exercise is also the first one written to the HIPV coding convention, which the project assignments also require.
UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter. “Asynchronous” means there is no clock wire between the two devices. The transmitter sends bits on a single wire, called TX, and the receiver has to work out on its own when each bit starts and ends. This only works because both sides agree in advance on two things:

title: 6  Sixth exercise: UART transmitter
text:
The baud rate, the number of bits per second. Common values are 9600, 19200 and 115200 baud. Every bit lasts exactly one bit period, 1 / baud rate.
The frame format, which describes how each byte is wrapped on the wire.


6.1.1 The UART frame
When nothing is being sent, the line sits at logic 1. This is called the idle state. Each byte is then sent as one frame:

Start bit. The transmitter pulls the line to 0 for one bit period. The falling edge from idle to 0 tells the receiver that a frame is starting.
Data bits. Usually 8 bits, sometimes 5 to 9. The least significant bit goes first.
Parity bit (optional). An extra bit for simple error detection. With even parity it makes the number of 1s in the data and parity bits even.
Stop bit. The line returns to 1 for at least one bit period (sometimes 1.5 or 2). This guarantees that the next start bit has a falling edge.

The frame format is written as a short code: data bits, parity (N for none, E for even, O for odd) and stop bits. The most common format, and the one used in this exercise, is 8N1: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. An 8N1 frame is 10 bits long, so a byte takes 10 bit periods.






Figure 6.1: One 8N1 frame carrying the letter H (0x48 = 0100 1000) at 115200 baud. The data bits are sent LSB first, so they appear on the wire in the order 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0.



Figure 6.1 shows the frame for the letter H. Its ASCII code is 0x48, or 0100 1000 in binary. Because the LSB goes first, bit D0 on the wire is the rightmost bit of the binary number. Reading the wire from left to right gives the binary number backwards.


6.1.2 Baud rate and clock cycles
Inside the FPGA, everything is measured in clock cycles. The Nexys A7 clock runs at 100 MHz, so the number of clock cycles in one bit period is
LIMIT = CLK_FREQ / BAUD_RATE = 100 000 000 / 115 200 = 868.06  ->  868
The division does not come out even, so the transmitter really runs at 100 000 000 / 868 = 115 207 baud. That is only 0.006 % fast. A UART receiver samples each bit in its middle (see the next section), so the two sides can differ by a few percent before a bit is read wrongly. With a slow baud rate and a fast clock, rounding errors like this one never matter.


6.1.3 How a receiver reads the frame
The receiver waits for the falling edge of the start bit. It then waits half a bit period, which brings it to the middle of the start bit, and checks that the line is still 0. After that it waits one full bit period at a time and samples the line in the middle of each data bit, and finally checks that the stop bit is 1. The testbenches in this exercise decode the TX line in exactly this way.
Sampling in the middle of the bit is what makes the scheme robust. Small differences between the transmitter and receiver clocks shift the sampling point a little on every bit, but it stays inside the bit as long as the total drift over a frame is less than half a bit.

6.3 Assignment
You will build the design in two parts:

Part A, the UART transmitter uarttx. It takes one byte and a start pulse, and sends the byte as an 8N1 frame at 115200 baud.
Part B, a message sender. Pressing the centre button BTNC sends Hello World! followed by a new line to the terminal.







Figure 6.3: Top-level design. A press of BTNC starts hellotxctrl, which feeds the message from msgrom into uarttx one character at a time.



Figure 6.3 shows the complete design. btnpulse turns a press of BTNC into a single clock-cycle pulse. hellotxctrl then steps an address through the message stored in msgrom. For each character it starts uarttx and waits until the frame is finished before moving on. The serial line goes to the USB-UART bridge and is also copied to Pmod pin JA1, so you can look at it with the oscilloscope. Two LEDs show when a message and when a single character are being sent.
The starter files are listed below. Files marked given are complete. Do not change them. The others contain the module interface and TODO comments that describe what to write.

6.3.1 Step 1: Create the project
Create a new Anvil project for the Nexys A7 100T, as in the tools intro:
mkdir uart_hello && cd uart_hello
anvil init --board Nexys-A7-100T
Copy all ten .sv design files into the project root, replacing the generated top.sv. Copy the two testbenches into tb/. You can download them all at once by running this command inside the uart_hello folder:
rm -f top.sv; B=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/laspp/digital_design_lab/main/code/06_lab; wget -q $B/{top,uarttx,uarttxctrl,baudgen,shiftreg,hellotxctrl,msgrom,btnpulse,flopenr,mux2}.sv && wget -q -P tb $B/{uarttx_tb,top_tb}.sv
It first removes the top.sv generated by anvil init. Otherwise wget would save the starter file as top.sv.1 next to it. The {...} part expands into one URL per file, and -P tb puts the testbenches into tb/. On macOS, install wget first with brew install wget.
The project should then look like this:
uart_hello/
  config.json
  Nexys-A7-100T-Master.xdc
  top.sv  uarttx.sv  uarttxctrl.sv  baudgen.sv  shiftreg.sv
  hellotxctrl.sv  msgrom.sv  btnpulse.sv  flopenr.sv  mux2.sv
  tb/
    uarttx_tb.sv
    top_tb.sv
Anvil compiles every .sv file in the project root, for both anvil build and anvil test. One module per file therefore needs no extra configuration. Just keep the design files in the root and the testbenches in tb/.


6.3.2 Step 2: baudgen
The baud rate generator is a counter that produces a one-cycle Tick once every bit period. It is the same idea as the prescaler from the fourth exercise and the 2 ms timer from the fifth, with one addition: a Clear input.
module baudgen #(parameter LIMIT = 868) (
  input  logic clk, reset,
  input  logic Clear,
  output logic Tick);

  localparam WIDTH = $clog2(LIMIT);
  localparam logic [WIDTH-1:0] LAST_COUNT = WIDTH'(LIMIT - 1);

  logic [WIDTH-1:0] Count;
endmodule

WIDTH and LAST_COUNT are already worked out from LIMIT. $clog2(868) is 10, because 2^10 = 1024 is the smallest power of two above 868. The cast WIDTH'(...) resizes the 32-bit result of LIMIT - 1 to WIDTH bits, so the comparison below has matching widths.
Write an always_ff block. When reset, Clear or Tick is high, set Count to 0. Otherwise increment it.
Drive Tick high while Count equals LAST_COUNT. Because the counter goes back to 0 on the cycle after Tick, one period is exactly LIMIT cycles.

Why Clear? A frame can start at any moment. Without Clear, the counter would be somewhere in the middle of its period when the start bit begins, and the start bit would be shorter than one bit period. The control FSM holds Clear high while it is idle. The counter therefore starts from 0 together with the start bit, and every bit of the frame is exactly LIMIT cycles long.


6.3.3 Step 3: shiftreg
The shift register holds the byte being sent and presents it one bit at a time, LSB first, on SerialOut.
module shiftreg #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic             clk, reset,
  input  logic             Load, Shift,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D,
  output logic             SerialOut);

This module is a datapath, so the convention asks for a structural description. Build it from the two generic cells, as the HIPV instruction fetch unit does for its PC register. Figure 6.4 shows the structure.






Figure 6.4: Inside shiftreg. The register feeds its own value back through a shift by one place. loadmux picks either the shifted value or the new byte, and datareg stores it only when Load or Shift is high. Because Load drives the multiplexer select, it has priority over Shift.



Follow these steps:

Assign ShiftedQ = {1'b0, Q[WIDTH-1:1]}. Every bit moves one place down and a 0 enters at the top.
Instantiate mux2 #(WIDTH) loadmux. It selects D when Load is 1 and ShiftedQ otherwise. Its output is NextQ.
Assign En = Load | Shift.
Instantiate flopenr #(WIDTH) datareg. It stores NextQ into Q when En is high.
Assign SerialOut = Q[0]. After a load, Q[0] is D0. Each shift brings the next bit into position 0.

The port names of the generic cells are D0, D1, S, Y for mux2 and clk, reset, en, D, Q for flopenr.


6.3.4 Step 4: uarttxctrl
The control FSM sequences the frame. It has four states, one for each part of the frame, as shown in Figure 6.5.






Figure 6.5: State diagram of uarttxctrl. Each state shows the level it puts on the serial line. A transition label reads condition / output pulse.




IDLE. The line is 1. When Start arrives, the FSM pulses Load so the shift register captures Data, and moves to START.
START. The line is 0 for one bit period. On Tick, move to DATA.
DATA. The line carries SerialBit. On every Tick, one bit is finished. If it was not the last bit, pulse Shift to bring up the next bit and stay in DATA. After the last bit, move to STOP.
STOP. The line is 1 for one bit period. On Tick, pulse Done and return to IDLE.

A 3-bit counter BitCount keeps track of which data bit is on the line. It is cleared in START and incremented on every Tick in DATA. LastBit is high while it equals DATA_BITS - 1, which is 7.
The skeleton gives you the state type and the state register, written in the same style as the HIPV core’s FSMs:
  typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, START, DATA, STOP} statetype;

  statetype             State, NextState;
  logic [CNT_WIDTH-1:0] BitCount;
  logic                 LastBit, TxNext;

  // state register
  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) State <= IDLE;
    else       State <= NextState;

Write the bit counter as described above.
Write the next state logic as an always_comb block with a case on State. Start with NextState = State, so that every state holds unless a transition applies, and add a default branch.
Write a second always_comb block that sets TxNext: 0 in START, SerialBit in DATA, and 1 in IDLE and STOP.
Register the line: Tx <= TxNext on every clock edge, with reset value 1.
Drive the remaining outputs with assign:




Output
High when




Load
in IDLE and Start is high


Shift
in DATA, Tick is high and it is not the last bit


BaudClear
in IDLE


Busy
in any state other than IDLE


Done
in STOP and Tick is high









Do not infer latches in the next state logic



An always_comb block describes combinational logic only if it assigns every signal on every path through the block. If some path leaves NextState unassigned, the signal has to keep its old value on that path. Combinational logic cannot remember anything, so synthesis adds a latch, a level-sensitive storage element, to hold the value. A latch is not what you meant. It makes the timing unpredictable, and the design can behave differently on the board than in simulation.
This happens easily in an FSM. The following next state logic infers a latch:
always_comb
  case (State)
    IDLE:  if (Start) NextState = START;  // no else: NextState is not assigned
    START: if (Tick)  NextState = DATA;
    ...
  endcase
In IDLE without Start, nothing assigns NextState. Two habits prevent this:

Give every signal a default value at the top of the block, before the case. NextState = State; means “stay in the current state” on every path that does not assign a transition.
Always add a default branch to the case, even when the listed states seem to cover every value.

The same applies to TxNext here and to the next state logic of hellotxctrl in Step 8. Check the output of anvil build. When Yosys finds a latch, it prints Latch inferred for signal ... with the signal’s name. If you see this message, look for the path that does not assign that signal.


Why register Tx instead of assigning TxNext to it directly? TxNext is combinational logic driven by the state register and the shift register. When both change on the same clock edge, the output of that logic can glitch for a few nanoseconds before it settles. On an internal signal that would not matter, because the next clock edge only samples the settled value. The TX line, however, goes off the chip to a receiver that does not share our clock. A short glitch to 0 on an idle line looks exactly like the start of a frame. A flip-flop output changes only once per clock edge, so registering Tx makes the line clean. The reset value of 1 matters for the same reason: the line must be idle, not 0, from the moment the FPGA starts.
The register delays the line by one clock cycle. It delays every bit by the same cycle, so the bit lengths are unchanged.


6.3.5 Step 5: uarttx
Now connect the three blocks as shown in Figure 6.6.






Figure 6.6: Inside uarttx. The FSM controls the baud rate generator and the shift register, and puts the right level on Tx for each part of the frame.



module uarttx #(parameter CLK_FREQ = 100_000_000, BAUD_RATE = 115_200) (
  input  logic       clk, reset,
  input  logic       Start,
  input  logic [7:0] Data,
  output logic       Tx,
  output logic       Busy, Done);

  localparam LIMIT = CLK_FREQ / BAUD_RATE;

Instantiate baudgen #(LIMIT) baud.
Instantiate shiftreg #(8) datareg with .D(Data) and .SerialOut(SerialBit).
Instantiate uarttxctrl #(8) ctrl.

All internal signals are already declared. Connect every port by name, as the convention requires.


6.3.6 Step 6: Simulate the transmitter
Simulate the transmitter before going further. At 115200 baud a frame is 8680 clock cycles long, which is a lot to scroll through in a waveform viewer. The testbench avoids this by instantiating uarttx with BAUD_RATE = 10_000_000, so LIMIT is only 10 cycles. Because the baud rate is a parameter, you do not have to edit the design to make simulation faster, unlike the timers in the previous exercise.
anvil test tb/uarttx_tb.sv
gtkwave tb/uarttx_tb.vcd &
The testbench sends five bytes and decodes the Tx line with the mid-bit sampling described earlier. A working transmitter prints:
OK:    sent 0x55, received 0x55
OK:    sent 0xa3, received 0xa3
OK:    sent 0x48, received 0x48
OK:    sent 0x00, received 0x00
OK:    sent 0xff, received 0xff
PASS: all frames correct
If the design never produces a frame, the testbench stops after 200 µs with a FAIL: timeout message instead of running forever. In the waveform, check that:

Tx is 1 after reset and between frames.
The start bit, every data bit and the stop bit are each exactly 10 clock cycles long.
For 0x55 (0101 0101), the line alternates 0, 1, 0, 1, … after the start bit, since D0 is 1.
Busy is high for the whole frame, and Done is a single-cycle pulse at the end of the stop bit.



6.3.7 Step 7: msgrom
The message is stored in a small read-only memory, written as a case statement that maps an address to a character.
module msgrom (input  logic [3:0] Addr,
               output logic [7:0] Char);
The message is Hello World! followed by two control characters. Carriage return (CR, 0x0D) moves the terminal cursor to the start of the line, and line feed (LF, 0x0A) moves it down one line. Together they start a new line, so each press of the button prints the message on its own line. That makes 14 characters, at addresses 0 to 13.
The skeleton already has H, e, CR, LF and the default branch. Fill in addresses 2 to 11 using an ASCII table. These are the codes you need:



Character
ASCII

Character
ASCII




space
0x20

l
0x6C


!
0x21

o
0x6F


W
0x57

r
0x72


d
0x64

e
0x65





6.3.8 Step 8: hellotxctrl
The message sender is a second FSM. It walks the address through the 14 characters and hands each one to uarttx.
module hellotxctrl #(parameter MSG_LEN = 14) (
  input  logic       clk, reset,
  input  logic       Send, TxDone,
  output logic [3:0] Addr,
  output logic       TxStart, Busy);

  typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, START, WAIT} statetype;
Figure 6.7 shows the state transitions.






Figure 6.7: State diagram of hellotxctrl. START lasts exactly one cycle and starts a frame. WAIT holds until uarttx reports TxDone, then either fetches the next character or ends the message.




IDLE. Wait for Send. When it arrives, clear Addr to 0 and move to START.
START. Pulse TxStart for exactly one cycle and move to WAIT. At this moment msgrom is already showing the character at Addr on Data, so uarttx loads the right byte.
WAIT. Wait for TxDone. If the character just sent was the last one (Addr equals MSG_LEN - 1), go back to IDLE. Otherwise increment Addr and go to START for the next character.


Write the Addr register. It is cleared on reset and when Send arrives in IDLE, and incremented when TxDone arrives in WAIT.
Write LastChar and the next state logic in the same style as in Step 4. Keep the default assignment and the default branch, so you do not infer a latch (see the warning in Step 4).
Assign TxStart (high in START) and Busy (high in any state other than IDLE).

This is a handshake between two FSMs. hellotxctrl does not need to know how long a frame takes. It just waits for uarttx to report that it is done. If you change the baud rate, the sender keeps working without any change.
Note that Send is only acted on in IDLE. Pressing the button again while the message is being sent does nothing.


6.3.9 Step 9: top
The board wrapper connects everything to the pins. Two parts of it are already written.
Reset. The red CPU_RESET button is active low: it reads 0 while pressed. The modules expect an active-high reset, so top simply inverts it with assign Reset = ~cpu_resetn;. You do not need to press reset after programming. The FPGA starts with every flip-flop at 0, which is already the IDLE state of both FSMs.
btnpulse. This module turns a press of BTNC into a single-cycle pulse. A flip-flop remembers the button’s level on the previous cycle, and Pulse = BtnSync & ~BtnPrev is high for exactly one cycle when the button goes from released to pressed. No matter how long you hold the button, the sender gets one Send pulse. Before the edge detection, the button passes through two more flip-flops (BtnMeta, BtnSync). You will learn why signals from outside the clock domain need them later in the course.
Complete top.sv:

Instantiate hellotxctrl #(14) sender, with .reset(Reset) and .Busy(MsgBusy).
Instantiate msgrom rom.
Instantiate uarttx #(100_000_000, 115_200) tx, with .Start(TxStart), .Data(Char), .Tx(uart_tx), .Busy(TxBusy) and .Done(TxDone).
Assign ja1 = uart_tx, led[0] = MsgBusy and led[1] = TxBusy.

Use Figure 6.3 to check the connections.


6.3.10 Step 10: Simulate the system
The system testbench resets the design, presses BTNC once, and decodes the uart_tx pin at the real 115200 baud:
anvil test tb/top_tb.sv
The whole message takes about 1.2 ms of simulated time, which is around 120 000 clock cycles. That takes only a few seconds to simulate. A working design prints:
Received: "Hello World!\r\n"
PASS: message received correctly
If a character is wrong, the testbench prints it as it was received, so you can see which entry of msgrom or which bit of the transmitter is off. To keep the waveform file small, the testbench records only the top-level pins in tb/top_tb.vcd. Use uarttx_tb from Step 6 to look inside the transmitter.


6.3.11 Step 11: Pin constraints
Map the top-level ports to the board pins in the project’s .xdc file:
## Clock signal, 100 MHz
set_property PACKAGE_PIN E3 [get_ports {clk}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {clk}]
create_clock -period 10.0 [get_ports {clk}]

## CPU_RESET button (red, active low)
set_property PACKAGE_PIN C12 [get_ports {cpu_resetn}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {cpu_resetn}]

## Button BTNC
set_property PACKAGE_PIN N17 [get_ports {btnc}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {btnc}]

## USB-UART bridge: UART_RXD_OUT is driven by the FPGA
set_property PACKAGE_PIN D4 [get_ports {uart_tx}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {uart_tx}]

## Pmod JA pin 1, copy of uart_tx for the oscilloscope
set_property PACKAGE_PIN C17 [get_ports {ja1}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {ja1}]

## LEDs
set_property PACKAGE_PIN H17 [get_ports {led[0]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[0]}]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN K15 [get_ports {led[1]}]
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[1]}]


6.3.12 Step 12: Build, program and open a terminal
Build the design and program the board:
anvil build
anvil program
To see the message you need a serial terminal on your computer, set to 115200 baud, 8N1. The FT2232 chip shows up as two serial ports. The first one is the JTAG programmer, and the UART is the second one.

Linux & WSL. The UART is usually /dev/ttyUSB1. Open it with screen /dev/ttyUSB1 115200 or picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyUSB1. If you get a permission error, add yourself to the dialout group (or uucp on Arch) and log in again.
macOS. Run ls /dev/tty.usbserial-*. You will see two names that differ only in the last character. Pick the second one (ending in 1 or B) and open it with screen /dev/tty.usbserial-XXXXXXXX1 115200.

To quit screen, press Ctrl-A, then K, then Y.
Press BTNC. The terminal should print Hello World!, and every further press prints it again on a new line. The whole message takes only 1.2 ms, so LED0 and LED1 flash too briefly to see. They are still useful: an LED that stays lit means an FSM is stuck. If something is wrong, use these hints:

Nothing appears. Check that you opened the second serial port and that uart_tx is on D4, not C4. Make sure the red CPU_RESET button is not stuck and that the design was built with your latest code.
Garbage characters appear. The baud rate does not match. Check the terminal setting and the uarttx parameters in top.sv.
The characters are right but come out in the wrong order, or one is missing. Run top_tb again and check hellotxctrl. The address is probably updated on the wrong condition.
LED0 stays lit after a press. hellotxctrl is stuck in WAIT because it never sees TxDone. Check the Done output of uarttxctrl and its connection in top.sv.
Sometimes the message appears twice for one press. Keep reading, this is the first question below.



6.3.13 Step 13: Look at the frame on the oscilloscope
The serial line is also on pin 1 of the Pmod JA header. Connect the oscilloscope probe to JA pin 1 and its ground clip to JA pin 5, as described in the oscilloscope appendix.

Set the timebase to 10 µs per division and the vertical scale to 1 V per division.
Set the trigger to a falling edge at about 1.5 V, and use single trigger mode. The first falling edge of a message is the start bit of H.
Press BTNC and compare the captured frame with Figure 6.1.
Use the cursors to measure the width of one bit. It should be 8.68 µs.

If your oscilloscope has a serial decode function, it can also read the frame for you. Choose the RS232 (UART) decoder on CH1 and set it to 115200 baud, 8 data bits and no parity. The oscilloscope then prints each character under the waveform.

title: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial
text:
7.1 Software and firmware
In this exercise you meet the HIPV SoC: a small RISC-V computer that runs on your Nexys A7 board. You will find where its code lives, write a C program for it, build that program, run it first in simulation and then on the FPGA, and watch it blink the LEDs and talk over the UART.
Until now every design in this course was hardware that you described in SystemVerilog. This time the hardware is already written. What you write is software: a C program that the processor executes.
Two words are used throughout this chapter:
You write software, and the build turns it into firmware.
crumbs: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial

title: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial
text:
Software is the C code you write, together with the toolchain that compiles it. It lives in the sw/ directory of the HIPV repository.
Firmware is the finished memory image (firmware.hex) that is built into the FPGA bitstream. After the build, the program is part of the hardware, much like the program of a router or a microcontroller.
crumbs: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial

title: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial
text:
7.2 The HIPV SoC
HIPV is a system on chip (SoC): a processor, memory and peripherals connected by a bus, all inside one FPGA. Figure 7.1 shows the parts.






Figure 7.1: Block diagram of the HIPV SoC. Green blocks are inside the FPGA design, red blocks are board pins and connectors.




The core executes the RV32I instruction set (32-bit RISC-V, integer instructions only) in a five-stage pipeline.
The crossbar routes the core’s two bus ports, one for instructions and one for data, to the right peripheral, based on the address.
The RAM holds both the program and its data. It is initialized with the firmware when the FPGA is configured.
The UART, timer and GPIO are the peripherals. The program uses them by reading and writing addresses, which is called memory-mapped I/O.

On the board, the GPIO connects to the 8 slide switches and the 8 LEDs, and the UART connects to the USB cable that you also use to program the board.

title: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial
section: 7.3 Step 1: Get the project and the tools
text:
7.3 Step 1: Get the project and the tools
Clone the HIPV repository:
git clone https://github.com/RatkoFri/HIPV-SoC.git
cd HIPV-SoC
You need the tools from the first exercise (Anvil, sv2v, openFPGALoader) and a RISC-V compiler (riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc). How you get them depends on your computer:







Your computer
Recommended setup




Ubuntu / Linux
Install the tools natively (gcc-riscv64-unknown-elf is the Debian and Ubuntu package name), or use the Docker image. Everything, including programming the board, works from the same terminal.


macOS and Windows with WSL
Use the Docker image to build, and program the board from the host. See the box below.



The repository provides a Docker image that contains all the tools. Every make target in this chapter can be run inside the container by prefixing it with docker-, for example make docker-sw APP=blink. Build the image once with make docker-build; it downloads several gigabytes. See README.md in the repository for details.






macOS and WSL



Docker on macOS and on Windows runs containers inside a virtual machine, and that machine cannot reach USB devices. The container can therefore build the firmware and the bitstream, but it cannot program the board. The workaround is to split the flow in two. The commands are the same on macOS and in a WSL terminal:

Build inside the container:
make docker-fpga APP=blink
Program the board from the host with openFPGALoader, outside the container:
brew install openfpgaloader     # macOS, once
make program-host
On WSL, install openFPGALoader in your WSL distribution instead of using brew, and forward the board’s USB connection to WSL first (the WSL only steps in the first exercise). WSL does not see USB devices on its own.

In the rest of this chapter, replace make APP=blink all with the two commands above, and likewise for your own program. Compiling (make APP=blink sw) and simulation (make run) need no USB, so they work unchanged in the container.

text:
7.4 Step 2: Memory map and peripherals
The processor sees everything as addresses. Table 7.1 lists the address map from config/hipv_soc_pkg.sv.



Table 7.1: HIPV address map.





Block
Base address
Size




Code window (RAM)
0x0000_0000
64 KiB


Data window (RAM)
0x1000_0000
64 KiB


UART
0x2000_0000
4 KiB


Timer
0x2000_1000
4 KiB


GPIO
0x2000_2000
4 KiB






The code window and the data window are two views of the same physical RAM. The core fetches instructions through the first and accesses data through the second. The linker script keeps code and data in different parts of it.
The registers that the exercise uses are listed in Table 7.2. The complete list is in sw/bsp/hipv.h.



Table 7.2: The registers used in this exercise.










Register
Address
Meaning




GPIO_OUT
0x2000_2000
Drives the LEDs. Can be read back.


GPIO_IN
0x2000_2004
The state of the switches.


UART_TX
0x2000_0008
Writing a byte starts sending it.


UART_STATUS
0x2000_0010
Bit 0 is set when the transmitter is idle.






In C, a register is a volatile pointer dereference. In sw/bsp/hipv.h:
#define REG32(addr) (*(volatile uint32_t *)(addr))
#define GPIO_OUT    REG32(GPIO_BASE + 0x00)
So the C statement GPIO_OUT = 0xFF; is nothing more than a store word instruction to address 0x2000_2000. That store goes through the crossbar to the GPIO, which turns on the LEDs.
You will rarely use the registers directly. The board support package (BSP, sw/bsp/bsp.h) wraps them in small functions:



Function
What it does




uart_init(baud)
Sets the UART speed


uart_putc(c), uart_puts(s)
Send a character, send a string


print_hex8(v)
Send a byte as two hexadecimal digits


print_udec(v)
Send an unsigned number in decimal


gpio_write(v)
Write the LEDs


gpio_read_in()
Read the switches


timer_start()
Start the free-running 64-bit timer


delay_cycles(n)
Wait for n clock cycles



There is no C library. You cannot call printf, malloc or strlen, and the BSP is all the support there is.
