7.6 Step 4: Run it in simulation first
Synthesizing for the FPGA takes minutes, so it is a slow way to find a bug. The repository can also run a program in a simulation of the whole SoC. From the example directory:
make run
The simulator boots the SoC with build/blink.hex as the RAM contents, watches the UART output pin, decodes the serial frames into characters and compares them to expected.txt. The run is long because every character takes thousands of clock cycles.
Use simulation for logic errors, such as wrong output text, and the board for what only the board can show, such as the real timing and the switches.

section: 7.7 Step 5: From firmware to the FPGA
text:
7.7 Step 5: From firmware to the FPGA
On the board, the build flow takes the firmware, builds the SoC with it and programs the FPGA. From the root of the repository:
make APP=blink all
(On macOS and WSL, use the two-step flow from the box in Step 1 instead.)
APP is the name of a directory in sw/examples/. The all target runs three stages, which you can also run one by one:







Command
What it does




make APP=blink sw
Compiles the software into blink.hex


make APP=blink fpga
Builds the bitstream with blink.hex as the RAM contents


make APP=blink program
Programs the board with the existing bitstream



The default board is the Nexys A7-100T. If you have the Nexys A7-50T, add BOARD=nexys-50t.
Open a serial terminal on the board’s USB serial port with 19200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. The name of the port depends on your system. Check which new device appears when you plug the board in:








System
Port
Terminal program




Linux
/dev/ttyUSB1 or similar
picocom -b 19200 /dev/ttyUSB1


macOS
/dev/cu.usbserial-...
screen /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX 19200 (leave screen with Ctrl-A, then K)


Windows (also when you build in WSL)
COM3 or similar, see Device Manager
PuTTY, with connection type Serial



On Windows the serial port belongs to Windows, not to WSL, so open the terminal there even if you built the firmware in WSL.
You should see blink followed by the changing patterns, and the LEDs should chase one another at one step per second.

7.7.1 What is different from a normal program
Compare this to a PC, or to the Microblaze flow of earlier years, where a program was downloaded to the running system:

The firmware is part of the bitstream. The RAM is initialized with blink.hex while the FPGA is configured (the INIT_FILE parameter of the RAM). There is no separate program download.
Every change to the C program means a new bitstream, and so another synthesis run. This is why simulation first is worth the time.
The clock must match. The software knows the clock frequency from CPU_HZ (50 MHz by default, which is what the SoC runs at) and uses it to compute the UART speed and the delays. If you change the clock in the hardware, you have to give the same CPU_HZ to the software build. A mismatch does not stop the build. It shows up as garbled text in the terminal and wrong delays.

title: 7  Seventh laboratory exercise: HIPV SoC tutorial
text:
7.8 Laboratory exercise
Write a program that runs forever, and once per second:

toggles all eight LEDs (all on, then all off, and so on), and
reads the eight switches and prints the state of both on one line over the UART.

A line of the output looks like this:
LED=FF SW=A5
LED=00 SW=A5
LED=FF SW=A1

7.8.1 Steps

Create a directory for your program inside sw/examples/, and copy the starter files main.c and Makefile into it:
mkdir sw/examples/lab07
cp main.c Makefile sw/examples/lab07/
The Makefile expects to be one level below sw/examples/, like the other examples.
Complete the three TODO items in main.c. The functions you need are in the table in Step 2.

For the toggle, remember that the GPIO output register should always be written a full word at a time.
print_hex8 takes a uint8_t, so cast the 32-bit values.

Build and try it in the simulator. In main.c, temporarily set DELAY_CYCLES to a small value such as 1000 (a full second is too long to simulate), then run make run in sw/examples/lab07. There is no expected.txt for this program, so the run only prints what the program sent over the UART. In simulation the switches are not pressed, so expect SW=00. Set DELAY_CYCLES back to CPU_HZ before going on.
Run it on the board from the repository root: make APP=lab07 all. Open the serial terminal, move the switches, and check that the printed SW= value follows them within a second.



7.8.2 Questions

What is the address of the register that gpio_write writes to? Find the matching store instruction in build/lab07.lst and write down the instructions the compiler generated for it.
How many instructions does your main loop contain? Look at the listing. The core needs about three clock cycles per instruction. How long does one pass take apart from the delay_cycles call? Is it significant compared to the one-second delay?
What would happen if you changed CPU_HZ in the Makefile to 100000000 but did not change the hardware? Why does the build not report an error?
After you change one constant in main.c, which steps of the flow have to be repeated for the change to show up on the board?



7.8.3 Optional extensions

Print the switches in binary instead of hexadecimal (eight 0 and 1 characters).
Let the switches choose the behavior: for example, SW[0] stops the toggling, and SW[2:1] selects the period (0.25, 0.5, 1 or 2 seconds).
Use timer_get() to print the time since start-up in each line.
Read docs/ADDING_A_SLAVE.md in the repository and sketch how you would add a new peripheral, such as a seven-segment display, to the SoC.

8.3 Testbenches
HIPV is verified with cocotb and Verilator: the design is simulated by Verilator, and the test itself is a Python program that drives the design’s inputs and checks its outputs. Each directory under tb/ is one testbench:

a Makefile, which says which RTL files to compile and which module is the top (TOPLEVEL);
one or more test_*.py files, each holding several tests (Python functions marked @cocotb.test()).

Run a testbench with make in its directory. Useful options:



Option
Effect




TESTCASE=<name>
run only one test


WAVES=1
write a waveform, dump.vcd



The homework uses testbenches at three levels. The level tells you what is simulated and what plays the rest of the world.









Level
Directory
Simulated RTL
The testbench plays




Unit
tb/unit/<module>
one module (mul, idu, ieu, …)
the modules around it: it drives every input port directly, cycle by cycle


Core
tb/core
the CPU pipeline hipv_core only: fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback, forwarding. No RAM, bus or peripherals.
the two memories: Python models of an instruction and a data memory on the core’s OBI bus ports, with configurable wait states


SoC
tb/soc (via make run in sw/)
the complete system hipv_soc: core, crossbar, RAM, UART, timer, GPIO
the outside world: it loads a compiled C program into the RAM and decodes the characters the program prints on the UART pin



A failure at a lower level is easier to debug: the unit testbench points straight at one module, while a failed SoC test only tells you the printed text was wrong. Work upwards: unit first, then core, then SoC.

8.3.1 Unit level: tb/unit/mul (Task 2)
Toplevel: your mul module alone. The testbench plays the Execute stage. It pulses Start with the operands, waits for Done, then raises Ack. Every result is compared with hw1_model.py.
To check the interface contract in the header of mul.sv, the testbench does two things on every operation:

it drives random values on A, B and Funct3 after the Start cycle, so a unit that does not capture its operands fails;
it checks that Busy, Done and Result follow the contract.








Test
What it checks




test_edge_cases
all four instructions on 12×12 operands chosen to break naive designs: 0, 1, all ones, 0x80000000, 0x7FFFFFFF, values on the 16-bit seam such as 0x0000FFFF and 0x00010000


test_random
400 random operations; Ack is delayed by 0–3 cycles, and Done/Result must hold steady meanwhile


test_latency
logs the Start → Done latency of each instruction (record it for the report); fails if it exceeds 8 cycles


test_back_to_back
a new Start in the cycle right after Ack



cd tb/unit/mul && make


8.3.2 Unit level: tb/unit/idu and tb/unit/ieu (regression and Task 1)
These test the Decode and Execute stages. You will change both modules. The original tests must keep passing: they check that the RV32I behavior is unchanged. They write the existing ALUControl codes as numbers, so keep those codes unchanged (see Task 1).

tb/unit/idu: field extraction, decoding of every RV32I instruction class, register file read/write and bypass, flush, back-pressure.
tb/unit/ieu: all ten ALU operations, branch conditions and targets, jal/jalr, lui/auipc, forwarding selection, back-pressure, bubbles.

Both testbenches also contain tests for the homework:

tb/unit/idu: test_zba_zbb_decode and test_zba_zbb_same_funct3_distinct check that every new instruction decodes to something different from the RV32I instruction with the same funct3 (and from each other). test_zmmul_decode checks that mul, mulh, mulhsu and mulhu are flagged for the multiplier, and that div, divu, rem and remu do not write a register. These tests do not depend on how you encode the control signals.
tb/unit/ieu: test_alu_encoding checks the ALU codes in hipv_pkg.sv against the table in Task 1. test_zba, test_zbb_logic_with_negate, test_zbb_min_max and test_zbb_count drive the new codes into the Execute stage and compare the ALUResultE with a reference model. The tests read the codes from hipv_pkg.sv, so the constants must have the names given in the table.



8.3.3 Core level: tb/core
Toplevel: hipv_core, the pipeline without the SoC around it. Each test:

builds a short program in Python with the encoders in rv32i.py (li(1, 0x80000000), andn(3, 1, 2), sw(3, 0, 10), …);
places it in the Python instruction memory and runs the core for a fixed number of cycles;
checks the values the program stored in the Python data memory against hw1_model.py.

A failure prints the instruction, its operands, the stored value and the expected value, for example andn(0x00000001, 0x00000000) = 0x00000000, expected 0x00000001. “Never written” means the store never happened; usually the pipeline hung, or the store went to the wrong address.
The Makefile selects the test file with MODULE:








Command
File
Contents




make
test_hipv_core.py

8.3.4 SoC level: sw/hw1/check and sw/hw1/bench
Toplevel: hipv_soc, the complete system. make run in a program directory compiles the C program, loads the binary into the SoC’s RAM, simulates the whole system and captures everything the program prints on the UART (tb/soc/test_sw.py).

sw/hw1/check is self-checking. Every instruction runs on all pairs of 12 operands and is compared with a reference written in plain RV32I C, so the reference does not depend on your hardware. The run passes if the printed text matches expected.txt exactly. A failing line shows how many results were wrong and the first one:
sh1add  OK
min     FAIL 23/144  a=80000000 b=00000001 hw=00000001 ref=80000000
sw/hw1/bench prints a table and does not check anything (see Software on the SoC).

A run simulates 4 million cycles and takes about half a minute.
Testing on real hardware. sw/hw1/check is the binary to flash to the board — sw/hw1/bench is simulation/report-only. Build and program it with:
make APP=hw1/check all              # build, synthesise, flash
The Makefile builds for the Nexys A7 100T by default (BOARD ?= nexys-100t). If you have the Nexys A7 50T, select it with the BOARD variable:
make BOARD=nexys-50t APP=hw1/check all   # same build, for the Nexys A7 50T
To test your design on the board instead of simulating it with make run, give the target explicitly. For example, on the Nexys A7 50T:
make APP=hw1/check BOARD=nexys-50t fpga      # build the firmware and the bitstream
make APP=hw1/check BOARD=nexys-50t program   # flash the existing build
fpga only builds; program flashes the board without rebuilding; all runs sw, fpga and program in one go.
The only valid values are nexys-100t and nexys-50t. Any other value stops make with an “Unknown BOARD” error. You can also set the board once for your shell session with export BOARD=nexys-50t, which saves repeating it on every command.
After flashing, open a serial terminal at 19200 8N1 (see docs/FPGA.md). The program runs once at boot and stops — it does not loop. If you don’t see output (the terminal was opened after it already ran, or you want to see it again), press the CPU_RESETN button (the red one) to restart it; you do not need to reflash.


8.3.5 Existing SoC and FPGA testbenches (regression)
tb/soc (with plain make: a small assembly program exercising every peripheral) and tb/fpga (the board wrapper) must still pass at the end. They don’t test the new instructions; they show you haven’t broken the system.


8.3.6 Hidden tests
The provided tests are a good start, not the whole story. Your design is also graded with additional hidden tests of the same kind and at the same levels: more operand values, other instruction sequences, other memory timings. Write your own tests for the corner cases you can think of (see Rules).

8.5.1 Instructions

All four use opcode OP. The divide instructions div, divu, rem and remu (funct7 0000001, funct3 1xx) are not part of Zmmul. HIPV has no illegal-instruction trap yet, so they must execute as nops: no register is written.


8.5.2 Required architecture
Constraints. The whole design may contain exactly one multiplication operator, with two 16-bit unsigned operands. A multiply must finish (Done) at most 8 cycles after Start.






Use the * operator



Implement the 16×16 multiplier with the SystemVerilog * operator, for example P = A16 * B16; with 16-bit unsigned operands. Do not write your own multiplier out of shifts and adds. The synthesis tool maps * onto the FPGA’s dedicated multiplier hardware, and this single * is the one multiplication operator the design may contain.


Idea. Split each operand into 16-bit halves, A = AH·2¹⁶ + AL (and the same for B). Then
A·B = A_L·B_L  +  (A_L·B_H + A_H·B_L)·2¹⁶  +  A_H·B_H·2³²
so four 16×16 products, each shifted to its weight, give the full 64-bit product. The unit computes one of them per cycle and sums them in a 64-bit accumulator.
Algorithm. The unit executes Table 8.2 once per multiply. A, B and Funct3 are valid only in the Start cycle, so everything the later steps need must be stored there.



Table 8.2: Multiplication with one 16×16 multiplier. All four · use the same multiplier.

In every step, Step selects the operand halves and the shift:

the half of A is Step[1] ? AReg[31:16] : AReg[15:0];
the half of B is Step[0] ? BReg[31:16] : BReg[15:0];
the shift is 16 · (Step[1] + Step[0]) bits.

mul returns the low word of the sum, mulh, mulhsu and mulhu the high word.
Signed operands. The four partial products are unsigned, so the sum above is the product of the unsigned bit patterns. A signed 32-bit value equals its unsigned bit pattern minus 2³² when bit 31 is set:
Asigned = Aunsigned − a31·2³²
Work out from this what correction mulh and mulhsu need, and what AccInit must be for each of the four instructions. Explain in your report why the correction only affects the high word, and why mul needs none. One clean way to apply it costs no extra cycle: look at the Acc ← AccInit operation in the Start cycle.
Structure.

mul.sv holds the datapath. Its ports are fixed and must not change, because the unit testbench depends on them. The header of mul.sv defines the contract for Start, Ack, Busy and Done; read it carefully.
mulctrl.sv holds the state machine. Its ports are up to you.



8.5.3 Timing of the mul interface
The diagrams below show the reference design, which needs 5 cycles from Start to Done: one Start cycle, four partial-product cycles (Step 0–3) and one cycle presenting the result. Your design may be faster or slower, up to 8 cycles. One column is one clock cycle. x means “don’t care”: the value can be anything, and the testbench drives random values there.
Result taken at once (Ack in the first Done cycle). Cycle 0 is the Start cycle:






Figure 8.1: Result taken at once: Ack in the first Done cycle. Dashed lines mark don’t-care values.




Cycle 0: Start is high. This is the only cycle in which A, B and Funct3 are valid, so everything the unit needs from them is captured at the end of this cycle.
Cycles 1–4: one partial product per cycle, selected by Step.
Cycle 5: Done is high and Result holds the product. Ack in the same cycle means “taken”.
Cycle 6: the unit is idle again, and a new Start may come.

Result taken later (the pipeline is not ready yet). Done and Result hold until Ack:






Figure 8.2: Result taken later: Done and Result hold until Ack.

The contract above already implies three states. The control unit below is one straightforward way to implement it. Other designs are fine as long as they keep the contract.

Transitions:

IDLE → BUSY on Start. In that same cycle the datapath captures the operands, remembers whether the low or the high word is wanted, and loads the accumulator with its starting value. The step counter is cleared.
BUSY → BUSY while Step ≠ 3. Each cycle adds one shifted partial product to the accumulator and increments Step.
BUSY → DONE when Step = 3. The last partial product is added, so the accumulator holds the full 64-bit result from the next cycle on.
DONE → IDLE on Ack. Without Ack the unit stays in DONE and keeps the result.

So mulctrl needs only Start and Ack as inputs, and gives the datapath Busy, Done, an accumulate enable and Step.


8.5.5 Connecting it to the pipeline
The multiplier lives in the Execute stage (ieu.sv). Three questions guide the integration:

How does Execute hold an instruction? At the moment, Execute is ready whenever it is empty or the Memory stage accepts (ReadyE = ~ValidEReg | ReadyM). A multiply has to stay in Execute until its result is ready, and must not be offered to Memory (ValidE) before that. Change ReadyE and ValidE so that the handshake does this. The rest of the pipeline then stalls on its own.
This is what the reference design looks like when the Memory stage is free (ReadyM = 1). The multiply enters Execute in cycle 0 and leaves it in cycle 5. The addi behind it waits in Decode, and the Memory stage sees bubbles meanwhile:






Figure 8.4: Reference design with ReadyM = 1: the multiply holds Execute for six cycles while addi waits in Decode.



Where does the result go? Forwarding takes the newest value from the Memory stage (ForwardDataM) and from Writeback. If the product leaves Execute on the same path as an ALU result, forwarding works unchanged. Explain why in the report.
When may the multiplier start? This is the subtle one. Your multiplier uses the forwarded operands in its Start cycle, while an ALU instruction uses them in the cycle it leaves Execute. Read the comment on PCSrcE in ieu.sv and the section “Branches and jumps” in IEU.md. Then think about what ForwardDataM contains while a load in the Memory stage is still waiting for its data.

Conditions for Start and Ack. Both signals are generated in ieu.sv, and each is the AND of several conditions:








Signal
Condition
Why




Start
a valid instruction is in Execute (ValidEReg)
a bubble must not start the multiplier



that instruction is a multiply (MulE)
ALU instructions never use the unit



the multiplier is not busy (~Busy)
Start is a one-cycle pulse that is only legal while Busy = 0; without this term the unit would restart on every cycle that the multiply stays in Execute



the operands are final
the multiplier captures A and B in this one cycle, so a wrong forwarded value cannot be fixed later. Question 3 above asks which signal tells you this.


Ack
a valid multiply is in Execute and the unit reports Done
there is a result to hand over



the Memory stage accepts it (ReadyM)
Ack is the handshake between the multiplier and the Memory stage. The result leaves Execute in the same cycle, so it is consumed only if Memory takes it.



Two consequences:

Done and Result stay stable until Ack. If Memory stalls, the multiply waits in DONE with its result, and the multiplier is released only in the cycle the result moves on (the second waveform above).
The Ack condition is the same condition under which ValidE is offered to Memory and ReadyE rises. Use it in both places, so the multiplier and the pipeline never disagree about whether the instruction has left.

cd tb/core && make MODULE=test_zmmul    # core level: the multiplier in the pipeline
cd sw/hw1/check && make run             # SoC level: both tasks from C

9.1 Equipment
This appendix covers the two pieces of lab equipment you will connect to the FPGA board whenever an exercise asks you to probe a signal directly, starting with the oscilloscope extension in the PWM RGB exercise. The same equipment and the same Pmod probing convention come back again in the SoC verification lab later in the course.
Simulation only shows how a design behaves in an idealized model. Real hardware adds effects simulation cannot show you: clock jitter, I/O delays, signal integrity issues, and interaction with external peripherals. Measurement equipment lets you check timing, frequency, and duty cycle against the actual signal coming off the board, not just the one your testbench predicts.

9.2 Connecting probes to the FPGA board
Several exercises route the signal to observe out through the JA Pmod header, using pin 1 as the signal and pin 5 as ground. The pinout is:


Connect the oscilloscope probe’s ground clip to the GND pin (pin 5) of the JA Pmod header.
Connect the probe tip to the signal pin (pin 1) of the JA Pmod header, for example the pwm_out signal from the PWM RGB exercise.
Also connect the FPGA board’s ground to the oscilloscope’s ground, so both share a common reference point.


Set the probe’s attenuation switch to 1X. A 10X setting attenuates the signal before it reaches the oscilloscope and will distort your reading.

If an exercise also asks you to compare against a reference signal from the signal generator, connect the generator’s output (CH1) to the oscilloscope’s second channel (CH2) with a BNC cable.

title: 9  Appendix: Using the Oscilloscope and Signal Generator
text:
9.3 Using the Rigol DHO914 oscilloscope
When you power on the oscilloscope, the main screen displays the waveforms captured on each channel.

The yellow box next to the RIGOL logo in the lower left corner shows which channel is currently selected, CH1 in the image above. Press a channel’s button on the front panel to select it. Each channel has its own vertical scale, coupling, and position settings.

9.3.1 Adjusting the display
The waveform grid’s horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is voltage.


The Sec/DIV knob sets the time scale, how much time one horizontal grid division represents.
Each channel’s Volts/DIV knob sets that channel’s voltage scale, how much voltage one vertical grid division represents.
Each channel’s Position knob, and the Horizontal Position knob, move the waveform on screen without changing its scale. Use them to center a waveform for a closer look.
The Auto button automatically picks scale and position settings for whatever signal is connected. It’s a good starting point when you aren’t yet sure what the signal looks like.
The Run/Stop button freezes the current acquisition. Press it again to resume capturing.



9.3.2 Measuring signal parameters
Press the Measure button (or the Measure knob, to the left of the Auto button) to open the measurement menu.

Measurements are grouped into three categories:

Vertical: voltage-related measurements such as Vmax, Vmin, Vavg, Vpp, and Vrms.
Time: time-related measurements such as Frequency, Period, Rise Time, Fall Time, and Duty Cycle.
Other: delay, phase, and similar cross-channel measurements.

Select the parameters relevant to what you’re verifying. For a PWM signal that is usually Period, Freq, and +Duty.

Close the measurement menu once you’ve made your selections. The chosen measurements stay on screen on the right side of the waveform display and update live as the oscilloscope keeps capturing.

9.4 Using the DG912 Pro signal generator
The DG912 Pro outputs sine, square, triangle, pulse, noise, DC, and arbitrary waveforms through two channels, CH1 and CH2. Most exercises only need CH1.

For each channel you can set:


Waveform type: square, sine, triangle, ramp, pulse, noise, DC, or arbitrary.
Frequency: press FREQ, enter the value on the numeric keypad, and confirm with ENTER.
Amplitude: press VPP to set the peak-to-peak voltage, or OFFSET to set the DC offset the waveform is centered around. An offset of 0V means the waveform swings between +VPP/2 and -VPP/2. The Ampl/HighL button switches between VPP/offset and high/low voltage level entry, whichever is more convenient for the levels you need.
Duty cycle (square waves): press DUTY, enter a percentage from 0 to 100, and confirm with ENTER. Duty cycle is the fraction of one period the signal spends high. 50% means high for half the period and low for the other half.
Phase: press PHASE and enter a value in degrees from 0 to 360, the shift of the waveform relative to a reference point in time.

Once configured, enable the channel’s output by pressing the gray area next to it. It lights up yellow when the output is active.

To match a 3.3V FPGA output level on a reference channel, set VPP to 3.3V and Offset to 1.65V, so the signal swings from 0V to 3.3V instead of being centered on 0V.
